transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hello, Dr. [Name]. Thank you for seeing me. Well, I... I guess I came in today because I just can’t seem to get this out of my head, and it's really starting to wear on me. It’s my face. Specifically, right down here around my jaw and my neck. I just can’t stop seeing this... this awful sagging, this really uneven spot right along the jawline. 

I look in the mirror before I leave for work—I work in personal care, you know, helping out elderly folks, so I’m always interacting with their families and the visiting nurses—and it's just right there, staring back at me, making me look so lopsided. And I know they see it too. I mean, people will tell me it looks normal, or that they don't even know what I'm talking about, but they’re just being polite, aren't they? They have to say that. Because I know what I see, and I feel like it is absolutely the very first thing anyone notices when they look at me. 

It's not just at work with the families and the nurses, either, but everywhere I go. Even on Sundays. I walk into church and I can just feel people’s eyes dropping right down to my neck, looking at how uneven and saggy it is. I try to pull my collar up or fix my hair around it to hide it, but it just consumes my mind all day long, wondering who is looking at it and what they’re thinking... I just can't stop focusing on it, no matter what I'm supposed to be doing.
Can you describe what you see when you look at your jaw and neck in the mirror? Do you think others would notice the same thing if they looked at you without knowing what you were referring to?

Well, when I look in the mirror... it's just this heavy, drooping skin right here, especially on the left side. It pulls my whole face down. It makes me look so asymmetrical, like one side of my face is just melting away. I can see the exact line where it sags, right where the jawbone should be sharp and clean, but instead, it's just this... this pouch of skin. And the neck! It's like turkey wattles, but worse, because it's so uneven. I’ll stand there for twenty, maybe thirty minutes just pulling the skin back with my fingers, trying to see what I used to look like, what I *should* look like. I try different lighting, too. The bathroom light is the worst, it casts these shadows that just highlight every single flaw, but even in the natural light by the window in the living room, it’s still there. It's undeniable. 

And as for other people... honestly, doctor, I don't see how they couldn't notice it. I mean, it's right there on my face. It's not like a scar on my arm that I can just cover with a long sleeve. Like I was saying before, the families of the folks I take care of, the nurses coming in and out... I see their eyes dart down to my neck. They might not say anything, because people are polite, aren't they? They don't want to be rude to the woman taking care of their mother or father. And the people at church, too. We have this greeting time where everyone shakes hands, and I just feel so exposed. I try to wear scarves, even when it's warm, or high-collared shirts, but I feel like that just draws more attention to it sometimes. 

My sister, she tells me I'm crazy, that she doesn't see anything at all, that I look fine for my age. But she has to say that, right? She's my sister. But I know what I see. I see it every single day, and it's just so obvious to me that I can't imagine anyone else looking at me and not seeing exactly what I see. It’s just this glaring, awful defect, and I feel like it's the very first thing that registers in someone's brain when they meet me.
Do you find yourself repeating certain behaviors, like checking the mirror, touching your face, or adjusting your clothes, because of your concerns about your jaw and neck?

Oh, yes. Yes, all the time. It's honestly like I can't stop myself, even when I know I need to get going. Every single morning, right before I leave for work—or even if I just have a quick meeting with one of the nursing supervisors at the agency—I get stuck in this terrible loop. I'll get dressed, and then I just keep going back to the bathroom mirror. I'll stand there and fix my collar, pulling it up just a fraction of an inch, and then I'll try to arrange my hair so it falls exactly right over that awful sagging spot on my neck. 

But then I'll step away, and I'll think, 'Wait, does it look too obvious that I'm trying to hide it?' So I go right back into the bathroom to check again. And it's not just the bathroom mirror, either. Once I finally force myself to walk out the door and get into my car, I can't just start the engine. I have to pull out my phone and open the camera—you know, the front-facing one—just to take another look. The lighting in the car is different than the house, and I just panic thinking about how it's going to look to the families when I walk up their front steps in the daylight. I'll sit there in the driveway, angling the phone, adjusting my collar all over again.

And my poor daughter... she still lives at home with me, she's working and has her own busy life, but I am always bothering her with this. Before I leave, I'll track her down in the kitchen or call her out of her room and ask, 'Honey, does this look strange? Can you see it? Is my neck showing too much on this side?' She gets so exasperated with me, bless her heart, because she's trying to get ready for her own day and I'm asking her the same questions every morning. 

Doing all of this... the mirror, the hair, checking the phone, asking my daughter over and over... it just eats up so much time. I've actually been late to my clients' houses more than once because of it. The home care agency is very strict about punctuality, and I hate being late, I really do. I've always prided myself on being reliable for these elderly folks, they depend on me to be there on time for their medication and breakfast. But I just can't bring myself to drive away from the house until I feel like I've hidden my neck as best as I possibly can, even if it means I'm rushing and stressed the whole drive there. I just get so caught up in fixing it that I completely lose track of the clock.
Does this concern about your jaw and neck cause you a lot of emotional distress, or make it hard for you to function normally in your daily life, like at work or with your family?

Oh, it really does. It just... it takes over everything, Doctor. It really does. I mean, at the home care agency, they’ve actually asked me a few times recently if I wanted to step up, you know, maybe take on some of the supervisory pieces or help lead our monthly staff meetings. I’ve been there a long time, so it makes sense they’d ask, and honestly, the extra money would be nice. But I just... I had to say no. I keep passing up these chances. And it breaks my heart, it really does, because I know I’d be good at it! But the thought of standing up there at the front of the conference room under those awful fluorescent lights, with all the other aides and the nurses just staring at me... I know exactly where they’d be looking. They wouldn't be listening to what I was saying, they’d be looking right at my neck, right at this horrible sagging on my jawline. I just can’t bear the thought of being the center of attention like that. 

And even the parts of the job I *do* keep doing, it’s getting harder. Like the paperwork. We have so much logging to do for the clients, you know, charting their meals and their meds and their vitals, and I’ve actually fallen behind on it lately. Not because I don't know how to do it, but because I get so stuck in the morning, like I was telling you before, just trying to make myself look presentable enough to even walk out the door. By the time I get to my first client's house, I'm already stressed and running late, and then the paperwork just piles up while I'm trying to catch my breath and make up for lost time. 

And it's not just work, it's my personal life too. I used to be so active. I have this book club I’ve been going to for years with some ladies from the neighborhood, and a walking club that meets on Tuesday and Thursday mornings... well, I’ve just stopped going to a lot of it. I've missed the last three books, I think. Getting ready just feels like... like climbing a mountain. I'll think about having to pick out a shirt or a scarf that hides my neck, and doing my hair just right, and knowing I'll have to sit in someone's well-lit living room for two hours sipping tea while they all look at me... I just can't do it. I'll call and say I have a migraine or something. It's just too much effort, too much anxiety to face people. So I just stay home. It's... well, it's really lonely, honestly, but it's just easier than feeling like everyone is judging my face.

No other disorder in the list fits as comprehensively).
